values: Bhai Dooj: the god of death goes to his sister’s for a meal

Bhai Dooj falls today, Wednesday 11 November (Drik Panchang, New Delhi).

It is also called Yama Dwitiya. The story says Yamuna kept inviting her brother Yama home for a meal, and when he finally came on this day he gave a boon in return: a brother who eats at his sister’s home on this day is freed from the sufferings of Yamaloka. That is why a festival about siblings carries the name of the god of death.

Image: Yamuna, terracotta, Gupta period, 5th century, from Ahichchhatra, National Museum, New Delhi. Photo: G41rn8, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Sources: Drik Panchang; regional names from common usage in Bengal and Nepal.

Read Brahmi in five minutes: two words from Ashoka

This script went unread for centuries until James Prinsep cracked it in the 1830s. You can read two of its most famous words in the next five minutes.

Learn six letters and two small marks, and you can read dhaṃma and Piyadasi, words Ashoka had cut into rock and pillars in the 3rd century BCE.

Image: Major Rock Edict, Kalsi. Photo: Ms Sarah Welch, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Sources: Richard Salomon, Indian Epigraphy (1998); E. Hultzsch, Inscriptions of Asoka (1925).

Fact 009: Junagadh, a dam breach 420 cubits long

A dam breach 420 cubits long, as many broad and 75 deep: those are the numbers cut into a rock at Junagadh around 150 CE.

The inscription of the Mahakshatrapa Rudradaman says that in year 72 rain and swollen streams from mount Urjayat tore open the dam of the Sudarshana lake. It says Rudradaman made the dam three times as strong from his own treasury, without oppressing people with taxes or forced labour, and that his minister Suvishakha carried out the work. It also recalls earlier work on the lake under the Maurya kings Chandragupta and Ashoka.

Image: part of the inscription, plate from Epigraphia Indica vol. VIII (1905-06). Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

Source: F. Kielhorn, Junagadh Rock Inscription of Rudradaman, Epigraphia Indica VIII (1905-06), pp. 36-49.

Boli: Kaithi, the script of Bihar's courts

In 1880 one order made a scribes' script the sole script of Bihar's courts. Within thirty-odd years Devanagari had overtaken it.

Kaithi takes its name from the Kayasthas, the scribal community of north India. Lieutenant-Governor Ashley Eden ordered its exclusive use in Bihar's courts in 1880. By January 1881 Persian was barred and Kaithi or Devanagari were allowed. Bengal cancelled the order in 1893 under pressure from Devanagari's supporters and restored it in 1894. Kaithi stayed official until at least 1913, after which Devanagari became the preferred script.

The script wrote Bhojpuri, Magahi, Maithili, Awadhi and Urdu. Its mark is easy to learn: no line on top of the letters. A 1963 gazetteer for Purnea still called it "in vogue but declining in use". Since 2009 it has had its own Unicode block.

Image: printed Kaithi letters from E.B. Eastwick, A Concise Grammar of the Hindustani Language, 2nd ed., 1858. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

Source: Anshuman Pandey, Proposal to Encode the Kaithi Script in ISO/IEC 10646 (2007), pp. 1, 13-17, 23, which draws on Grierson, Jha and King; Unicode 5.2.

Fact 010: coins helped unlock Kharosthi

Two sides of a coin helped crack a lost script.

Indo-Greek kings such as Menander I struck coins with a Greek legend on one side and a Kharosthi legend on the other, giving the same royal name in both. In the 1830s James Prinsep and other scholars used such coins to begin working out the Kharosthi letters. The script ran mostly right to left.

Image: coin of Menander I, British Museum. Photo: PHGCOM, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Source: Richard Salomon, Indian Epigraphy (1998), pp. 210-212.

Chhath: the first arghya goes to the setting sun

Today, 15 November, the first arghya (offering) of Chhath goes to the setting sun; the second goes to the rising sun tomorrow at dawn.

Drik Panchang (New Delhi) lists Nahay Khay on 13 November, Kharna on 14 November, Sandhya Arghya today and Usha Arghya on 16 November, and says the festival is dedicated to Surya. Usha means dawn, and in the Rigveda she is a goddess: hymn 1.113 begins, “This light is come, amid all lights the fairest” (tr. R. T. H. Griffith, 1896).

Image: Surya, the Sun God, with Attendants. Bronze, Pala period, ca. 9th century, Bangladesh. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 1987.142.334. Public domain (CC0).

Sources: Drik Panchang, Chhath Puja 2026 (New Delhi); Rigveda 1.113, tr. R. T. H. Griffith (1896).

Heritage this week: five deadlines, the nearest on 19 November

Five deadlines for students and scholars of India’s past, the nearest on 19 November.

1. American Institute of Indian Studies fellowships (junior, NEH senior and early-career travel): apply by 19 November 2026. Non-US citizens qualify only through a US institution.
2. Jagiellonian University, Kraków: a two-year postdoctoral post, extendable by two, in VOICES, a European Research Council project on South Indian pattu song cultures, Malayalam preferred: apply by 21 November.
3. Dr Harisingh Gour Vishwavidyalaya, Sagar: one contract curator in the Department of Ancient Indian History, Culture and Archaeology, Rs 40,000 a month for up to 12 months: apply online by 30 November.
4. University of Zurich: professorship in the Cultural History of India, starting 1 August 2028: apply by 7 December.
5. Indian History Congress, 85th session, Puducherry, 26 to 28 February 2027: papers due by 7 February 2027; only members may submit, and new members enrol by 15 January 2027.

Each story, with its official source, is on the Talaash Heritage news page: talaash-heritage.pages.dev/news.html

World Heritage Convention at 54: India's 45 sites

54 years ago today, on 16 November 1972, UNESCO’s General Conference in Paris adopted the World Heritage Convention. India ratified it on 14 November 1977, and now has 45 properties on the World Heritage List: 37 cultural, 7 natural and 1 mixed.

Article 1 defines cultural heritage. Its first category, monuments, names “inscriptions, cave dwellings and combinations of features” alongside architecture, sculpture and painting. India’s first four sites, inscribed in 1983, were Agra Fort, Ajanta, Ellora and the Taj Mahal; the newest is the Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath (2026).

Image: Courtyard of the Kailasa temple (Cave 16), Ellora Caves, Maharashtra. Photo: Rohit Sharma, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Sources: Convention concerning the Protection of the World Cultural and Natural Heritage (1972), Article 1; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, States Parties: India.

UGC-NET December 2026: the 6% cut and your subject code

6%. In UGC-NET, the number of candidates declared eligible for Assistant Professor equals 6% of those who sit both papers, with the slots split by category.

To be counted at all you need at least 40% aggregate across the two papers (General and EWS; 35% for OBC-NCL, SC, ST, PwBD and third gender). Cut-offs are then set for each subject and category. The December 2026 exam has 87 subjects, among them Archaeology (67), Anthropology (07), History (06), Indian Culture (50), Linguistics (31), Museology and Conservation (66), Sanskrit (25), Pali (83) and Prakrit (91).

The paper: 150 questions, 300 marks, 3 hours, no negative marking. Exam city slip 23 November, admit card 7 December, exam 14 to 18 and 21 December 2026; you sit on the one date and shift on your admit card. NTA says dates may change, so check ugcnet.nta.nic.in.

Source: NTA, UGC-NET December 2026 Information Bulletin (as corrected, 16 October 2026); NTA public notices of 8 October, 27 October and 1 November 2026.
